Certain calls do not count toward these frequencies under § 1006.14(b)(3) — e.g., calls placed with the person's prior consent given directly to the collector within the following seven days, calls not connected to the dialed number, and calls to persons listed in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)–(vi). results.derivation_summary: Under §1692a(6), a person is a 'debt collector' if the principal purpose of its business is collecting debts, or if it regularly collects debts 'owed or due another' — plus a limited-purpose category (for §1692f(6) only) covering businesses whose principal purpose is enforcing security interests; the definition excludes creditors' own officers/employees, affiliated collectors, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and persons collecting debts they originated or that were not in default when obtained. A 'creditor' (§1692a(4)) is one who extends credit or is owed the debt, excluding one who takes assignment of a defaulted debt solely to collect for another, and a 'debt' (§1692a(5)) is a consumer obligation to pay money arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes. Henson holds that a company collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not collecting debts 'owed another' and so is not a debt collector under that prong (leaving the 'principal purpose' prong unaddressed), and Obduskey holds that a business doing no more than nonjudicial foreclosure is a debt collector only for purposes of §1692f(6). So coverage turns on whether the obligation is a consumer 'debt' and whether the entity collects for another or has debt collection as its principal business purpose.

The definition contains numerous exceptions, such as for creditors' employees, and has a more limited application for entities engaged only in enforcing security interests.

results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a), an action on any contract, obligation, or liability founded upon a written instrument must be brought within four years (with a special three-month limit for deficiency-type money judgments after a trustee's sale under a deed of trust or mortgage with power of sale). Once that four-year period has run, § 337(d) bars the creditor from filing suit, arbitration, or any other legal proceeding to collect the debt, and the period may be extended only under § 360 — i.e., by a signed written acknowledgment or promise, or by a payment of principal or interest, though no payment can revive a claim already barred. Other provisions may affect the period in particular cases: emergency rule 9(a) tolled limitations periods over 180 days from April 6, 2020 to October 1, 2020; 11 U.S.C. § 108(c) extends the period where a bankruptcy stay applies; § 361 bars claims already time-barred in the state or country where they arose; and 20 U.S.C. § 1091a eliminates any limitations period for covered federal student loan and grant debts.

edge_cases.scenario: A San Diego consumer on active duty in the Navy stopped paying a Chase credit card in 2019 and was deployed overseas for two of the intervening years. In 2026 she asks whether a debt buyer can still sue her on the account.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node never screens for military service. The SCRA, 50 U.S.C. § 3936, excludes the entire period of active-duty service from any limitations period running for or against a servicemember — tolling that can add years. Because no checklist item prompts the question, a servicemember (a very common consumer-debt population in California) would report only her last-payment date, receive a flat 'expired/time-barred' answer, and could forgo defending a suit that is in fact timely. The generic 'any other tolling not yet encoded' caveat is a passive disclaimer, not a screening question, and it runs in the dangerous direction — telling the consumer she is safe when she is exposed. Bankruptcy and federal student loans each got dedicated threshold screens for exactly this reason; SCRA tolling is at least as case-dispositive.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a store credit card in 2021 while living in New York, then moved to Los Angeles in 2023; the collection agency sues him in California Superior Court in 2026. The cardmember agreement contains no choice-of-law clause (or designates California).
edge_cases.gap_description: CCP § 361 borrows the foreign limitations period whenever the cause of action AROSE in another state and is time-barred there — it does not require a contractual choice-of-law designation. Both the checklist item and choice_of_law_note frame § 361 conjunctively around a contract that 'designates the law of another state,' so a consumer whose claim arose in a shorter-SOL state (e.g., New York's 3-year consumer-debt period under CPLR 214-i) but whose agreement is silent or designates California would be told the 4-year California period applies and the suit is timely. Interstate moves with trailing consumer debt are extremely common, and the error causes the consumer to abandon a complete, dispositive defense.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer made her last credit-card payment in March 2022, missed the April 2022 payment, and the issuer charged off and accelerated the balance in October 2022. In June 2026 she is served with a collection complaint filed in May 2026 and wants to know if it is time-barred.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist's dispositive fact is framed as 'date of last payment ... or date of default/breach if no payments were made,' which defaults an account with payment history to the last-payment date. On a revolving account, accrual actually runs from the breach/acceleration, which on a standard 180-day charge-off cycle can be up to six months later. Near-boundary inquiries are precisely when consumers ask this question, so the encoded default produces a false 'expired' conclusion (here, March 2026 vs. an actual October 2026 deadline) and could cause the consumer to default rather than answer. The accrual note's 'fact question this node does not resolve' hedge is contradicted by the checklist's own last-payment default rule.

gaps_found.scenario: A San Diego consumer on active duty in the Navy stopped paying a Chase credit card in 2019 and was deployed overseas for two of the intervening years. In 2026 she asks whether a debt buyer can still sue her on the account.
gaps_found.gap_description: The node never screens for military service. The SCRA, 50 U.S.C. § 3936, excludes the entire period of active-duty service from any limitations period running for or against a servicemember — tolling that can add years. Because no checklist item prompts the question, a servicemember (a very common consumer-debt population in California) would report only her last-payment date, receive a flat 'expired/time-barred' answer, and could forgo defending a suit that is in fact timely. The generic 'any other tolling not yet encoded' caveat is a passive disclaimer, not a screening question, and it runs in the dangerous direction — telling the consumer she is safe when she is exposed. Bankruptcy and federal student loans each got dedicated threshold screens for exactly this reason; SCRA tolling is at least as case-dispositive.

gaps_found.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a store credit card in 2021 while living in New York, then moved to Los Angeles in 2023; the collection agency sues him in California Superior Court in 2026. The cardmember agreement contains no choice-of-law clause (or designates California).
gaps_found.gap_description: CCP § 361 borrows the foreign limitations period whenever the cause of action AROSE in another state and is time-barred there — it does not require a contractual choice-of-law designation. Both the checklist item and choice_of_law_note frame § 361 conjunctively around a contract that 'designates the law of another state,' so a consumer whose claim arose in a shorter-SOL state (e.g., New York's 3-year consumer-debt period under CPLR 214-i) but whose agreement is silent or designates California would be told the 4-year California period applies and the suit is timely. Interstate moves with trailing consumer debt are extremely common, and the error causes the consumer to abandon a complete, dispositive defense.

gaps_found.scenario: A consumer made her last credit-card payment in March 2022, missed the April 2022 payment, and the issuer charged off and accelerated the balance in October 2022. In June 2026 she is served with a collection complaint filed in May 2026 and wants to know if it is time-barred.
gaps_found.gap_description: The checklist's dispositive fact is framed as 'date of last payment ... or date of default/breach if no payments were made,' which defaults an account with payment history to the last-payment date. On a revolving account, accrual actually runs from the breach/acceleration, which on a standard 180-day charge-off cycle can be up to six months later. Near-boundary inquiries are precisely when consumers ask this question, so the encoded default produces a false 'expired' conclusion (here, March 2026 vs. an actual October 2026 deadline) and could cause the consumer to default rather than answer. The accrual note's 'fact question this node does not resolve' hedge is contradicted by the checklist's own last-payment default rule.
